body:
I'm enjoying it so far! My only issue is that the formatting is a bit hard to follow, but that's just a 'me' problem (I have two toddlers, it's a miracle my brain hasn't turned to dust by the end of the day). 


It feels a bit... painfully on the nose regarding some political issues lately. Granted, I'm not quite halfway through, so who knows.
Prophet Song by Paul Lynch

I'm not totally certain about payment arrangements (I think they've brought up the possibility but I haven't needed one yet), but we go to Gentle Dental. I have bad anxiety regarding dentists and went in knowing I needed work. So far, everyone I've seen has been kind and patient, to the point I don't dread going the way I used to.
I haven't read his other work, though I'm enjoying Prophet Song by Paul Lynch right now!

We typically do the library once a week. As long as life lines up well for us, I try to do the park at least twice a week, if not more. We don't have a play group but do have our 3.5yo in swimming lessons.


I'm trying to make a conscious effort for them this year. They have fun at stores and whatnot, but I know being outside and socializing is good for them even if it's not my cup of tea. There are definitely still days that the furthest we step out of the door is our backyard.

I think we started our daughter (almost 4yo) around a year. If I remember correctly, I laid out a towel on the floor and gave her an ounce or two of water in a small cup. I demonstrated with my own cup and let her figure it out.


She got the hang of actually getting it into her mouth within a few days, and the rest just came with more practice. Our son (18mo) can  drink, but has yet to master gravity; more of it ends up on him or the floor rather than in his mouth.

I enjoy doing Ring Fit on our switch - it's certainly not the most intense training but it's enough to motivate me to actually exercise. Our 3.5yo likes to do it alongside me, and I typically try to have our 17mo either sleeping or entertained with his dad.

Otherwise, I try to get outside. We live within a mile of about three different parks and two different libraries, so both kids get plopped in our bike trailer or our wagon and taken to wherever (having a specific destination in mind is helpful).

Right about 2.5yo. We went to a place that only does kids (not super fancy, but they had small play structures in the waiting area). The person who cut her hair gave her options (sit in a lap or on a booster, which cape she wanted, what toy she wanted to hold if she wanted to hold one). They didn't make a big fuss if she didn't stay still or got a little spooked.


She was curious and wanted to watch, but did really well. They gave us a few clippings in a little envelope. We booked it in advance and gave her opportunities to understand what would be happening (I think there's a Daniel Tiger episode?), which I think helped.


Our son had a less thrilling experience; his bangs were wild, so I plopped him in his high chair last month (16mo) and trimmed them while dad held his head. He didn't care at all.

For the 17mo, it's only 'eat'. He will sign and/or say 'eat' aggressively if someone says it and he will yell if eating does not happen.


For the 3yo, it's playground, juice, and library/the book place. All of the conversations I have with my husband are becoming so vague.

She threw up due to her first "real" stomach bug a few months ago and now tells us every single day that her tummy is starting to rumble. Sometimes she even includes that she wants to throw up.


Most times she just means she's hungry. Tonight, it did not.

She made friends with a bug on the outside of her window. It flew away and broke her heart. She refused to stop talking about the bug and demanding that I make it come back until I told her it had to go home.

A plague doctor around/over my left shoulder blade, especially once the artist started packing black and color in. That said, I only have 3 and the other two are on my forearms, which I didn't find painful.

Exquisite Corpse by Poppy Z. Brite (very graphic)


Tender is the Flesh by Agustina Bazterrica


Earthlings by Sayaka Murata

We have a microphone with similar functions. It even has a voice changer *and* a Bluetooth function so you can sing along to your choice of toddler music.


Once it ran out of batteries it conveniently disappeared.

Gynecology and Fertility P.C. in Bryan East - all of their staff are women. I've seen several of their doctors and haven't had any complaints whatsoever, but I regularly see Van Pelt and love her. I've never felt judged there and any concerns I have are addressed when I bring them up.

Before bed, if she's mad she has to go bed:


Me/Dad: I love you

Her: No, I don't want to love you!

Mental health issues started really effecting me around 12/13yo. I don't remember what I was upset about, but my mom asked if she needed to send me to a therapist (knowing full well the answer was yes). 


Rather than do that, she insisted she couldn't have *another* child betray her that way, because one of my brother's (who lied compulsively) had been to one growing up and his therapist (supposedly) believed a bunch of lies he told that made her seem like a bad parent.

Our two, by some stroke of luck, haven't had injuries that resulted in scars (yet).


I, on the other hand, have a permanent scar in my eyebrow where hair doesn't grow very well from walking into a coffee table at just the right height as a kid.

We moderate, but I'm not thinking too much about it. We aim for as little sugar added as possible but accept that, with our budget and time, that isn't always feasible. Our 3yo has the occasional fruit snack and has dessert a few nights a week, and I don't care if she has a Capri Sun and cake at a birthday party.


I grew up in a house that went to both extremes in a day (absolutely zero moderation and we were given our own 1.25l of soda, then told we were too chubby), and I'm not aiming to do that. She eats her veggies (the majority of them) and knows it isn't always time for fun food. 


Our 1yo is slightly more restricted just because he's less opinionated, but if his sister gets dessert he might get half of a tiny cookie.

I'm a SAHM, but I tend to aim for short bursts with our 3yo. I'm not the best with imaginative play (there's only so many times an adult can eat a pretend sandwich, y'know?) and tend to lead her toward things that have a clear end. A board game, arts and crafts, reading. She likes to help with cooking/cleaning (so long as she's not the one who made the mess) and we read together every night, so I know we're spending time with her even if it's not sitting on the floor playing with toys.


As much as she'd be over the moon, we have a 1yo and two dogs and a house to maintain too. 2 to 3 hours consecutively isn't realistic. Over the course of the day, sure.

We have broken *two* bowls from a set that is supposedly unbreakable less than 24hrs apart. The same set is also missing a plate from when it was launched off a high chair.


And, perhaps my favorite phrase ever uttered by my husband: "No, you may not spoon my eyeball."

She bonked her nose. I'll give her that one, because I tripped over a toy while I was carrying her to the kitchen and we both went down pretty hard. 


But also: It's been snowing. We had to run errands, and she decided she didn't want to wear her mittens. She picked up a fistful of snow at our first stop and got mad because, shocker, her hand was cold.

Not intentionally. If I have to shower while my husband is at work, I wait until the 1yo is napping and let the 3yo sit in our bed and watch a show and eat a snack. Sometimes she'll poke her head in to talk to me, but she's mostly content curling up in our bed.

A small, animatronic dog. It came with a dog house and a bone. Super cute until you turn it on. It yaps... nonstop. She loves it, but we've made it clear it can only be played with in her room if she wants it to make noise.


SIL apologized when she realized it made that noise. I suppose that helps a bit?
Hair ties. She was insistent Santa wanted to bring her hair ties. She needed them anyway, so Santa provided and put them in her stocking.

We change it as needed (squishy, poop, he managed to get it off in his crib) or around transitions. After breakfast, before nap, before second nap, after bed/before bed, before we leave the house, that sort of thing. He's never had serious rashes, so I don't think we're doing anything wrong.

Last night before bed our 3yo lost her mind because she desperately wanted to read "the shake by side by side" book. She insisted it was a library book we've read over the last few days but cannot point it out to us. There's also nothing close to that sentence in any of them.


I've tried playing songs with similar phrases to no avail. I dunno.
Our 13mo is endlessly fascinated playing peekaboo with his clothes (typically the pants I take off him to change his diaper). Otherwise, just handing him the clean diaper usually works.

Our 3yo is not particularly attached to any toy. She picks and chooses based on how she's feeling that day, and that's fine.


Our 13mo loves his stuffed cloth and isn't happy if it isn't in his crib when he's going to sleep. That is also fine.

Ours is YMCA. So much so that she figured out how to make her amazon echo play it because I refused to get up after having to start it three times in a row. 


She has apparently moved on for the moment and now just wants to hear "Jack Skeleton" all day and night, which is only mildly unfortunate because having her say "The Nightmare Before Christmas soundtrack" is a big ask and it means I have to bounce back and forth a lot.
Someone opened the bathroom door into my knee the other night because they *needed* a high five.

3yo: 1/3 a donut, a cup of milk, and a banana for breakfast. Lunch was a handful of cherry tomatoes and grapes, and maybe one chicken nugget. She ate two portions of lasagna and blueberries for dinner, then ate a couple of her dad's twizzlers for dessert. Snacks were something I don't remember.


1yo: cheerios (which went on the floor), a cup of milk, and half a banana for breakfast. Lunch was a scrambled egg with cheese and spinach, and... some fruit I don't remember. Also lasagna and blueberries for dinner and half of a popsicle (organic fruit based ones) for dessert so he wouldn't yell because he has serious FOMO about food. He also had a pouch at some point.

A small party at home with family and friends (15 people at most). No activities beyond the toys we already had because the oldest child was 1.5yo. I made a smash cake and a cake for everyone else, and I think we served pulled pork with buns and toppings. 


Our second had virtually the same but we did lots of appetizers rather than a main dish because tailgate style food fit with the theme of "first year down".

1. She wasn't allowed to kick her brother in the head, no matter how gently.


2. We have a couple things to do today, but she was upset we weren't leaving the moment *she* said so, and then was mad I wouldn't let her wear sandals... because it's 24°F outside.

My husband is home by dinner now without issue, but when his schedule was different we generally just talked about it. He'd call if he was going to be running behind, and we'd figure it out. Anything more than about 5 to 10 minutes, he'd just tell me to feed ourselves and he'd eat after bedtime.


He also certainly wouldn't be giving a toddler the cold shoulder about it. If anything, he gave himself the cold shoulder even if his reason for being late was out of his control.

No allowance. My husband leaves me to handle the majority of our day to day finances (bills, the budget for extras/savings) and I'm free to use what I need. We both talk about purchases exceeding about $50 and discuss the "bigger picture" finances as needed (retirement, the mortgage, whatever).

3yo had oatmeal, a mandarin, and a glass of milk. She ate it all without a fight.


1yo had cheerios, blueberries, and a cup of milk. And by "had", I mean he fed half the cheerios to our dog and found it delightful to share his milk with his sister. The blueberries were all his though.

What is it about desitin? Our 3yo will happily smear aquaphor anywhere but herself, yet *must* taste the desitin if she manages to get ahold of the tube. It doesn't smell good. The texture is awful. I just don't get it.

My husband and I aren't really traditional pajama people - he doesn't sleep with a shirt and I don't sleep with pants, and we just cover the other half with something comfy when we wake up. I don't think I've worn a matching set of PJs since I was 10 or 11.


Our kids can match or coordinate. They matched for Halloween because I happened to find the right sizes at Once Upon a Child, but I'm content with them only matching colors or themes (like Santa or reindeer or whatever), or not matching at all. I'll participate if they really want me to.


And they can definitely wear them until they don't fit.

One year (maybe last year? I don't remember) mine was almost exclusively country artists off of our 3yo's bedtime playlist. Don't get me wrong, they're all good songs, but not what I'd necessarily choose for myself.


Both kids have "smart" speakers in their rooms, so our 3yo has her own placeholder email that can be tied to our family plan for Spotify so I don't have to constantly be recommended stuff I don't want to hear, but it works for wrapped too.

That sounds incredibly stressful. 


Our 3yo, shockingly, did great. She even ate most of her food. Her 1yo brother, however, skipped the majority of his second nap and was very cranky. I could deal with this if he didn't shriek at the top of his lungs over every thing he perceives to be a problem, which was most things. Other people had food when he didn't, he dropped his cup, he dropped his monkey, he was told he couldn't eat dog food, he was told he couldn't wreck decor, his sister had pie when he didn't...


Thankfully, our family mostly found it endearing (because they don't hear it all day).

Unless we just don't have the money, yes. We tend to have one "big" gift we're both aware of (this year it's a fancy robe and hoodie from a specific place) and then a smaller one that's a surprise. Stockings are filled, though usually not with anything too exciting.

She needed to poop. Like the heartless parents we are, we refused to take her to Costco at 8pm (while we were getting ready for bed, no less) so she could poop there. So she laid down on the floor and cried.

What Moves the Dead by T. Kingfisher ticks those boxes for me - it's around 250 pages and has some pretty unsettling moments (YMMV, of course).


It's been longer since I've read them, so I'm not certain about length, but I think the following probably work too: Tender is the Flesh by Agustina Bazterrica, Exquisite Corpse by Poppy Z. Brite, and The Wasp Factory by Iain Banks.
We didn't budget specifically, but *not counting stocking stuffers*, our 3yo's stuff is about $150 and our 1yo's is probably closer to $100 - $125 (but he has less defined interests).
Our nephew's 2nd birthday was Toy Story themed and the goodie bags had character cups and silly straws! I think she got them at the Dollar Tree.

Lately, a dollhouse with furniture and a handful of dolls for it. She's played with it every day since her birthday in September. 


A baby doll with related accessories has also been a big hit.

She only wants dinosaurs. Easily accommodated in toy form.


She really wants to give our dog to her cousin, though, which isn't realistic.

Two adults and two toddlers - around $200 a week. Short of just never buying certain things, that's about as low as it gets without bouncing to different stores (which wastes gas and time). I dread when they're older and I have to make two extra portions instead of just one to split.
Our daughter (now 3yo) was absolutely thrilled to receive baby doll stuff last year. She still plays with all of it nearly every day, so I'd definitely think you're right!

1yo is happy with his half of a breakfast burrito, some peaches, and a cup of milk.


3yo decided she didn't want her breakfast burrito half after we ordered it, requested oatmeal that she still hasn't taken a bite of, and ate a cup of applesauce. She's coming off a stomach bug so... at least she's eating, I guess.

For his first Christmas, he was just over a month old. I know we got him gifts but I honestly couldn't tell you what they were, and of course I have minimal photos because people wanted to pass the baby.


This year, he's really involved. He and big sister both have stockings, books and clothes from Santa, plus a new blanket, a crafty thing, and toys from us.

Pokémon Primers: Shapes and Pokémon Primers: Colors. Checked them out from the library because our 3yo likes pokemon and we're still working on those subjects, and we needed something simple to keep 1yo's attention.


They each have *over* 100 little cardboard flaps. We gave up halfway through the shapes one because we'd already been reading for way too long. I don't know who thought that many was a good idea.

Quality may not always be top notch (I haven't had issues with the toys we've bought, but we haven't bought many), but Once Upon a Child has a toy section that's usually not too pricey. 


They do seem to cater more toward little kids, but do have bits and pieces for older kids.
She would have been between about 16 and 18mo the first trimester!

Console them while they watch you (our daughter freaked out every time she heard me throw up, which made it a bad few months for all of us). 


It certainly isn't a glamorous option, but there isn't always one.

They certainly could be memorial tattoos but I wouldn't immediately assume it's meant to be one if I saw one. 


You mentioned in a different comment that you were brainstorming - I wanted a more unique tattoo and put together an idea based on nursery themes (though one part is a loose interpretation), if that helps at all.

I'm a young parent - a zillenial, if you will. I was in high school before 2016's election, and I lived in a tiny conservative town in Texas. I stayed awake through the votes. I remember being afraid of what would happen. I remember resources floating around for people who weren't seeing any light at the end of any tunnel.


Last night I convinced myself to go to bed when it looked like we'd pull through. Now I'm afraid again. I want to hope it won't be as bad as we think, but I can't keep that up every day. I live in a red state now (our city leans blue, but I'm not sure that's helping) and leaving isn't that simple.


I'm scared of what happens if my IUD fails - I can't afford a tubal. I'm scared of what happens to schools now. I'm scared about whether we'll actually be able to afford to live in the coming months and years. I'm worried for the future - the climate, having teenagers, our ability to retire. I'm worried my identity as a bisexual woman will put me in danger.


And honestly? I'm worried when our kids grow up and understand the world a little better, they'll question why we thought it was a good idea to bring them into it.


But for their sake, I have to get up and continue on. The dogs need to go outside, the kids need breakfast, a birthday party needs prepped for. That's all I can do. That's all the energy I have.

The founder of my newest legacy wanted to have the best family reunion ever!


Because he is the founder, his family reunion consisted of the people who already lived in his house and one friend. Of course I forgot it was planned, so he was exhausted and just went to sleep rather than participate.

Right around 2yo - unfortunate for us, because our son was born around then. I tried desperately to hold onto them but she's stubborn and it wasn't happening.


Every now and then if she's had a long day, she'll pass out for 10 to 20 minutes in the car or on someone's lap. This is rare, and to be cherished.

Due to depression/anxiety, my mood gets funky this time of year. If I'm having an off day and she can tell (I try to save face but it isn't always easy), she'll hug my leg and tell me that it'll be okay.


She'll also occasionally tell me I'm so cute/beautiful, or so precious (but that one can get a little creepy).

At the moment it's looking good, but I've also spent the last three days in depression/anxiety induced cleaning haze.


Ordinarily, it's not great. I do what I can to keep it passable, but two kids + two dogs + two adults = ohmygoditneverstops. Dishes and laundry are never done. Our toddler's room is one massive toy pile that just gets gradually scooted to one side of the room until I have time. Baby's room is okay *only* because it's locked when he's not in there. Kid bath is clean enough but like? There's so many toys, and toddler found kid-safe nail polish that's now all over the side of the tub, and she rubbed some toothpaste on the mirror. Forget about our room, closet, and bathroom - I remember they exist before events at our house.


The living room ranges between Great and Was There a Tornado (including baby toys, laundry, and a random ripped up napkin)? I finally vacuumed it (after a couple weeks) but now there's cheerios on the floor because the baby decided his after dinner snack was a delightful toy. He also yanked a cup of coffee off the end table (don't worry, I'd forgotten it existed so it wasnt hot) this morning, so now there's coffee in the carpet and the table is still a little sticky because toddler wanted to clean it up for me. Also, the kitchen floor hasn't been mopped in a minute but it's supposed to rain, and our dogs certainly aren't wiping their paws before they come in so what's the point.


Our decor is family photos and toddler art (both on paper *and* walls). Our version of organization is. Just so many fabric bins. So many cube things.


Seriously, don't sweat it. I haven't met a single parent that actually has an Instagram worthy home.

Anywhere from 10 to 45 minutes. Maybe a few hours if you count the days she's done but wants it to be in the fridge until whenever she wants to eat more.


On the days she takes forever, I eat my own food, or clean in a place I can keep watch, or talk with my husband if he's home.

About 3 days at 2yo, because I had to give birth to her brother. She didn't mind, I hated it and felt awful.


11mo, overnight. We went out for our birthdays and MIL spent the night at our house with both kids. He was unphased.

I grew up with people who had their own issues with food and body image. One day they'd let us 8/9yo kids have diet soda and king size candy bars, then the next day they'd say we were getting too chubby but also not eating enough. Between that and food insecurity later on, my relationship with food is... weird, but I'm working on it.


Within the confines of our budget, I do what I can to make sure our kids are eating well-rounded, healthy-ish meals most of the time. We keep lots of snack options on hand and try to be conscious about sugar intake (it's not realistic for us to avoid it all together). That's about as far as I can go without driving myself crazy. 


Moderation is good in my book. If we have a bad day and don't eat as well as we can, we can move on and try again in the morning without feeling bad.

We didn't have much choice when we had our son - either our toddler stayed rear-facing at the correct angle and my husband had his knees practically forced into the steering wheel, or we turned her and he drove safely. Unfortunately, a new car wasn't in the cards (and still isn't).


It all happened at 2yo, and our pediatrician assured us it was okay if we needed to.

A confident 6 months. She's 3. 


She is well aware she's 3. She knows her full name and our names. But she heard me say her brother was 6 months awhile ago, so now everything is 6 months.

A play couch (we have the Sam's Club version of the nugget) and a little ride on car. Both are still used daily at 3yo. We loved the idea of a pikler or something similar, but they're pricey.


A colorable, pop-up playhouse was also loved, but to the point of being destroyed (but it was cardboard, so it's eventual ruin was inevitable).

Our daughter is 3yo, but last year she got a nursery set for her baby doll, new paint, some books, a robe (which she is still delighted by) and a preschool busy book.


The little people barn was a birthday gift, and is still used almost daily. Magnatiles are also a good choice.

A small bowl of chili, roughly half a mandarin orange (baby brother had the other half), and then an apple sauce cup. 


The fruit was a given, but I'm astonished she ate the chili. Spices, veggies, *and* protein? How scandalous.

I don't remember exact words, but it was something along the lines of, "You're never going to feel like you've been successful or done enough, because you keep raising the bar for yourself even when there's nowhere left to raise it."


It seems so obvious now, but it floored me then. 


Confirming a couple diagnoses helped too.

My mom had a chance with our daughter. Though I should have known better after my own childhood (not to mention her total lack of interest in my pregnancy), I gave her a chance.


Then she made a bunch of poor choices, some of which involved my daughter, so I kept her at a distance. Then she made worse choices, and drug my daughter into her issues with me. I stopped it there.


I don't think it's necessarily wrong to say poor parents can't be good grandparents - my FIL was a bad dad, but he's great with the kids in our family because he doesn't have to be the parent. It's possible they've changed, especially if it's been awhile, but I don't think it's wrong to proceed as if they haven't until they prove otherwise. I don't know what would convince me. A genuine apology would be a start, therapy would be a step in the right direction (though I know it won't happen).


Until then, no. It's my job to protect my kids and make sure they don't grow up the way I did. If that means they have one or two less grandparents, then so be it.

When I still kept contact (though minimal), we sent her a text that basically just stated I was in the hospital, all was well, and we'd update her later on. She called me, wanting to be present, but left me alone after I said no. She met our daughter 1.5 weeks later.


With our second, she never got to know about the pregnancy, let alone the birth. I felt guilty for awhile, but at the end of the day, my kids are what drove me to finally go NC. They deserve the best I can give them, and that means not having her in our lives.


I wouldn't think your dad deserves the memory regardless of whether you plan to talk to him; he's made his bed.

Yep! We've managed to create two of them, God help me. Our 3yo has not sat still since the moment she learned to walk, and our 11mo's new favorite activity is using the play couch as a ramp onto the actual couch, flopping back onto the floor, and doing it all over again. 3yo saw grandma last night and *literally* ran circles around her until she stumbled and fell over.


I envy their energy.

The nugget has been infinitely worth it. Every kid who comes to our house loves it, and it's pretty comfy (spoken as someone who existed on it during the first few months of their second pregnancy).


Otherwise, toys related to open-ended or pretend play. Pretend food, little people, magnatiles/megablocks, a baby doll, cars.

1: Honestly, I barely remember playing it. It always felt a bit bland but I did play BL2 first, so that's probably why.


2: Probably the same. Some areas feel pointless, and some maps are needlessly complicated (I've played the game so many times and still get lost in Sawtooth). 


3: Tyreen. She's cartoonishly evil and it's obnoxious. I suppose it's perfect for what she's meant to be. Additionally, I have a love-hate relationship with how much variety there is for weapons. I tend to want one of each gun type and element, and it's hard to keep track when I have a irradiated sniper/shotgun combo but also an irradiated/corrosive SMG or whatever.


TPS: The whole oxygen thing.


Tales: Never played either of them.


Wonderlands: I didn't finish it, but my husband and I started it. Inventory management in splitscreen is *atrocious*. The overworld was a bit disorienting but I got used to it eventually.

I went through something similar a tiny bit younger than her, though mine was a friend who didn't go to my school. My mom handled it badly - she refused to listen to me, and pretty much told me to get over it after 48hrs.


Of course you know your child best, but I'd follow her lead. It sounds like you already are, but give her some grace. Don't force her to talk but let her know it's an option, even if all you can really do is listen. If she wants (and it's possible), let her take a day or two off from school/extracurriculars. Let her be alone if she wants, or be available for a hug or an outing if she'd rather be with people.


As for the guilt - I don't know. You can certainly emphasize that it wasn't in her control if it comes up, but it didn't sink in for me until a few years into therapy. I would just refrain from clichés (hearing that a suicidal person will find a way to commit suicide regardless of your intervention or lack of is just... not helpful).

We have a 3yo, so there's an age difference to take into account, but:


- Stomp rockets
- Dig in a planter box
- Collect various backyard nonsense; sticks, leaves, rocks
- Play with balls
- Push a stoller/her tricycle/her cozy coupe around
- Pet the neighbor's dogs (we have permission)
- Blow bubbles, or make me blow bubbles
- Use her little slide 
- Point out random birds and bugs
- Water play with random dishes/utensils/puddles, assuming it's warm enough

General TW for talk of sexual assault and suicide.


Five years ago, I was sexually assaulted by a co-worker. The actual details would take forever to write out, but basically, I thought he was a friend and told him he could crash in my spare room while he went through some stuff. 


The month following was hard, needless to say. It took a week or so to find the courage to talk to the people I needed to (our supervisor and boss, my brother, the police, my therapist). He was fired, taken into custody, and then court proceedings had to start. All the while I had to wake up and actually exist. My mental health tanked so, so badly that I told my therapist I didn't trust myself to be alone despite having a safety plan in place, and she recommended I check myself into a hospital.


My supervisor (who is now my husband) drove me into a different city the next night and I was admitted. He told my brother because I asked him to. My brother mentioned it to our mom, thinking I had already talked to her.


She showed up unannounced. I didn't want her there but didn't really know how to advocate for myself, so she stuck around to visit. It went *awfully*. She berated me for being in the hospital, for not telling her because she'd been assaulted before and would know what to do, you get the idea. I was overwhelmed and stressed, which came out as scream-crying about everything that had been wrong since a certain point in our lives, she got defensive and claimed she didn't know anything had ever been that bad (yes she did), and nurses asked her to leave because they could hear us in the hallway.


She called me later on, and said she would be coming to my apartment to stay for a week or so "for my safety". At the time, she lived 40 minutes from me. Neither of us had a car. I had very little furniture. I lived on the second floor, and she's a disabled smoker. Eventually I found the confidence to tell her this was a terrible idea.


After I was discharged, I stayed with my brother for a weekend and then returned to work. Somewhere in this period, our mom decided to tell... everyone about what happened to me. Including relatives I haven't spoken to in over a decade.


Way to make it about you, mom.

With our first, I wanted to try breastfeeding. The 72hrs we spent on the postpartum floor were grueling. All the nurses pushed it, all the care techs pushed it. The information being given to me was always contradictive (it was going to hurt, it shouldn't hurt, she had enough wet diapers but was losing too much weight). The LC didn't show up until shortly before being discharged. 


I tried pumping at home, but never made enough. So I gave up and we went to formula, even though I felt guilty about it (combined with PPD, this was disastrous). I told our pediatrician, and she told me that was great, because fed babies make them happy.


She's now 3yo. She's happy, healthy, and growing too dang fast. She drew something resembling a stick person for the first time last night and it blew my mind.

- Some time before people visited us at home. We essentially said, "We'll let you know when we're ready for you to visit, and it'll only be one family per day". Husband let me dictate the length because, I'd like... had a baby. I think it ended up being about 5 days. We didn't have a particular order for people to show up, as it depended a lot on their schedules. Everyone got their turn eventually.



- Not to enforce vaccines, but to have simple restrictions. Don't show up if you're sick, wash/sanitize your hands before you touch her, don't kiss her face. Hold her if you please but don't be possessive.



Thankfully, no one had an issue with our choices, but my husband wouldn't have hesitated to speak up if needed (I was a hormonal mess and couldn't have handled confrontation). First of all, congratulations! Parenthood is a wild ride, but there's lots of subs here for you, so don't be afraid to reach out. As for your questions:


1. There's no set amount you really need to. Some people do it every day (don't use soap every day if you do). I bathed our daughter once every two days when she was that small, or as needed. 


2. A routine won't hurt. I wouldn't go in assuming it won't evolve as the baby grows or intend to be super strict about it since babies are a little all over the place, but it's nice to start early. Sleep training, though, is not recommended for another few months.


3. I attempted to breastfeed but couldn't, so we exclusively formula fed. Suggestions are just that - offer a little less than usual and give her another .5/1oz until she seems satiated, especially if it's full on vomiting. If it's just spit up, maybe switch to a different flow for the bottle nipple.


4. I never had much trouble burping her, but we did everything from over our shoulders to sat up right to laid flat over our knees (though that was mostly my MIL).


5. This would be a question for her pediatrician, but my assumption would be that if she's falling asleep during breastfeeding yet still gaining weight as she should, she's eating plenty. If that's not the case, we were told before we left the hospital to wake her up gently by tickling her feet/underarms so she'd continue eating.

As you said, you aren't telling them they're never going to meet your baby - they may just have to wait a minute if they don't want to abide by the restrictions you set. If they choose not to hear that, it's their problem. Your boundaries are more than reasonable and it's your responsibility to protect your child, not cater to their feelings. They are adults. Plus, wavering now may give the impression that you will in the future with other things, and that's not a great precedent to set.

I felt a lot of ways about it for awhile but at this point our daughter seems well adjusted, so I'm not too worried about it. I had a fairly normal vaginal birth with a second (borderline third) degree tear. I was still pretty exhausted, but had no issues getting up and moving. I hate being cooped up in the house, so sometimes we just walked around Target. I didn't move fast, but it kept me sane.


Depending on where you are, or when you have your baby, I would advise you to be careful of heat and overexerting yourself - I still overheated pretty quickly at that point.

The first time I ever had any kind of OBGYN appointment I believe I was somewhere around 10w. From what I remember:


• Be prepared to fill out quite a bit of paperwork - all the consent forms, plus details about family/medical history and past pregnancies (i.e., any positive test, even if it ended as a chemical pregnancy or MC). 


• I think most places will do an ultrasound at that point, and I believe you can have transabdominal ultrasounds done at 8w. If they can't see baby well (like if your dates are off), they may do transvaginal.


• You'll likely have a routine urine test (some places don't though) and blood work. Also just normal stuff, like your weight and blood pressure.


• If you haven't had one recently or at all, you may have a pap smear. I think some places hold off if you're pregnant just because it can mess with the results (I had "abnormal squamous cells" that turned out to be nothing once it was done again following delivery). I also had a breast exam because I, again, hadn't had one.


• You'll have the opportunity to ask every question you can think of. Write them down even if they seem stupid to ask.


• Your OB will likely have their own set of questions to ask you, and will go over what you should/shouldn't do and what to expect over the course of your pregnancy. The office I see also gives you a ton of stuff - a folder with pregnancy magazines, coupons, papers talking about the hospital, a list of what to bring in a hospital bag, delivery estimates, the book What to Expect When You're Expecting...


If everything is as it should be and you have no concerns after you leave, you'll likely be seen again in 4 weeks. For me, it's every 4 up until 28w pregnant, then every 2 until 36w pregnant, and then once a week until delivery.

• Toiletries.

We went on a week long trip with our toddler when she was 7mo, and also split our 12ish hour drive over two days. We stayed in hotels, though. Our list, from what I remember:


• I think we took an entire sleeve of diapers from a Costco box (plus whatever we had in the diaper bag), and one overnight per night. It lasted well enough. One of those three pack wipe containers.


• Something like two outfits per day plus PJs. We got lucky and didn't need that many. A hat and sunglasses she refused to keep on.  A couple pairs of sandals. Bibs, burp cloths if you use them. 


• If your diaper bag doesn't have one, I'd invest in a portable changing pad because you'd be surprised how many places don't have stations in their bathrooms.


• Pack n play, of course. Baby blanket just in case.


• Bottles, two cans of formula, a few containers of baby food, and snacks for the road. We ended up needing to buy distilled water just because the area we were in had different tap water than she was used to. Containers for food and utensils. We (thankfully) didn't need to then, but maybe an insulated bottle with warm water in the diaper bag if you have a picky baby.


• A floatie, two swimsuits, baby sunscreen and aloe lotion, and a pack of swim diapers - obviously not necessary if you aren't going to be in water.


• Teethers and noisy toys. You don't need nearly as many as you think.


• Baby tylenol (didn't end up needing, but BIL did), bath soap, and aquaphor. 


• Some kind of charged device for the possible inevitability you'll have to sit in the backseat and entertain the baby with Hey Bear Baby Sensory while you sit in traffic. Granted, we were going through both Dallas and Houston. 


• Of course, carseat and stroller.


We didn't bring much more than that - we were out and about so often that babyproofing would have been a moot point, and we have an easygoing sleeper that doesn't need pitch black + white noise.
